task.description: Step 2b re-gate (rework 2 of 3) of WF-03 for ISS-0418, per ORCH's dispatch: verify the rework-2 design against five points -- the rewritten determinism claim (§6.3) under all three call shapes and on_exit placement, the eight-vs-seven dispatch count, the three call-shape treatments (§6.2), the production-uncapped limitation's four required locations, and confirm the prior PASS items were not disturbed.

result.summary:
FAIL. One BLOCKER, carried through from re-derivation the prior gate could not have caught (it predates ORCH's option-three scope expansion). Four MINOR findings. The prior BLOCKER (false determinism claim) is confirmed genuinely fixed, not merely reworded, and the prior MAJOR (default-cap arithmetic) is confirmed genuinely fixed on re-derivation. This is a different failure than either prior gate found -- it lives specifically in the NEW §6.3.1 residual-risk analysis, using the design's own cited numbers against it.

=== 1. THE DETERMINISM CLAIM, RE-SPLIT (design section 6.3) ===

Both halves independently re-derived against real source, not the design's narrative.

CONCURRENT-ADMISSION HALF: TRUE, confirmed by direct verification, not assumption. (a) All three test files declare `use ExUnit.Case, async: false` -- confirmed by grep: call_timeout_test.exs:22, host_api_write_test.exs:34, plugin_handler_test.exs:15. (b) ExUnit's on_exit/1 mechanism is monitor-based (ExUnit.OnExitHandler), specifically designed to survive the test process being killed -- including by ExUnit's own per-test @tag timeout mechanism, which every :wasm_hang test in this suite sets to 180_000ms (confirmed present on all eight dispatch sites via grep). This is why on_exit/1, not a bare try/after, is the correct choice here (design's own reasoning, §6.2), and it holds under re-derivation: an on_exit registered before a possible mid-test kill still fires, releasing the lease, and ExUnit does not start the next async:false test until the current test's on_exit callbacks complete. So a lease is never held across a test boundary, and try_acquire/0 in test N+1 genuinely cannot succeed until test N's own dispatch has both returned (via invoke/2,3's own AC3 guarantee) AND released. This closes the exact race ISS-0418's recurrence log documents (a neighboring test's not-yet-cleaned-up leak still occupying a slot when the next test dispatches). CONFIRMED TRUE.

CUMULATIVE-WEDGED-SLOT HALF: correctly and honestly stated as NOT fixed (design agrees, §6.3/§0). This is not in dispute.

BUT: §6.3.1's claim that this residual risk is merely theoretical / not evidenced by ISS-0418's own recurrence record is WRONG, and this is the BLOCKER (below) -- not a defect in the true/false split itself, but in how the design characterizes the residual risk's real-world likelihood.

=== 2. THE COUNT: 7 tagged tests, 8 dispatches -- CONFIRMED EXACTLY ===

Read all three test files directly, matching the design's own §6.1 table row for row:
  - call_timeout_test.exs:76 (AC2): confirmed two sequential Wasmex.call_function/4 calls on the SAME pid (lines ~83-92 first call, ~103-110 second call on the now-wedged pid), both in try/catch :exit. Design's row 1 (2 dispatches) is exactly right.
  - call_timeout_test.exs:155 (AC5): confirmed one PluginInterface.invoke/3 call. Row 2 exactly right.
  - host_api_write_test.exs:460: confirmed one raw Wasmex.call_function/4 dispatch via start_instance/2's helper, try/catch :exit. Row 3 exactly right.
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:152 (AC5): confirmed one PluginInterface.invoke/3 call (line 163). Row 4 exactly right.
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:353 (REQ-170 AC1): confirmed one PluginInterface.invoke/2 call. Row 5 exactly right (verified via the AC1 describe block's own comment cross-reference, and the test body pattern matches AC3's sibling).
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:393 (REQ-170 AC3): confirmed the test reimplements Task.Supervisor.async_nolink/2 + Task.yield/2 + Task.shutdown(task, :brutal_kill) directly (lines 408-427), never calling PluginInterface.invoke at all -- one dispatch. Row 6 exactly right.
  - plugin_handler_test.exs:472 (REQ-170 AC4): confirmed two sequential PluginInterface.invoke/2 calls (lines 486, 489, timeout_ms 300 then 7_000). Row 7 exactly right (2 dispatches).
Total: 7 tagged tests, 8 dispatches. The design's reconciliation of the prior gate's "seven" (tagged tests) against ORCH's "eight" (dispatches) is correct terminology, not a fudge -- both counts are right for what they count.

=== 3. THE THREE CALL SHAPES (design section 6.2) -- CONFIRMED REAL, TREATMENT FITS EACH ===

Shape A (direct PluginInterface.invoke/2,3, rows 2/4/5/7): confirmed -- the test process IS invoke/2,3's caller, exactly the position S2/S8.1 already analyze for a production caller. Wrapping with try_acquire/0 before the call and on_exit-registered release/1 is architecturally identical to S2's already-verified reasoning (verified at the prior gate; re-confirmed here it still holds since invoke/2,3 itself is unmodified).

Shape B (row 6, plugin_handler_test.exs:393): confirmed by direct read that this test's own code IS structurally the same shape as invoke/2,3's internals -- the test process calls Task.Supervisor.async_nolink/2, then Task.shutdown(task, :brutal_kill) (line ~427) targeting the SPAWNED task, never itself. The test process is therefore never the killed one, matching Shape A's safety property exactly, just written out longhand. The design's treatment (acquire before async_nolink, release via on_exit after the existing brutal_kill call) is correctly placed outside the kill radius.

Shape C (rows 1/3, raw Wasmex.call_function/4): confirmed by direct read that no Task.Supervisor and no PluginInterface appear anywhere in either test's call graph -- the test process itself calls Wasmex.start_link/1 and Wasmex.call_function/4 directly, and observes its OWN exit via try/catch (confirmed: call_timeout_test.exs wraps both calls in `try ... catch :exit, reason -> ...`, matching ISSUE-FIXER's own finding that wasmex's client-side GenServer.call timeout crashes the CALLING process, not a spawned task). Since the test process survives its own exit via the catch, acquiring before start_link/1 and releasing via on_exit is safe and correctly reasoned -- there is no brutal-kill in this shape at all, so the crash-safety analysis is simpler than Shapes A/B and the design does not overstate it.

The deliberate exception (row 1's second call not taking a second lease): re-derived and CORRECT, not a hole. The second Wasmex.call_function/4 call in call_timeout_test.exs:76 (line ~103) targets the SAME already-wedged pid from the first call -- it is proving the Store stays wedged (design's own §1.2 finding), not dispatching a new, independent guest invocation. InvocationLease's contract (S5.2) admits INVOCATIONS, not raw NIF calls on an already-committed Store; wrapping this second call in its own try_acquire/0 would test something the primitive was never built to gate (a queued command on an already-occupied executor, not a fresh admission decision) and would misrepresent the assertion's own purpose. No coverage gap results: the first call already exercises the acquire/release path for this test's one genuine new-invocation event.

=== 4. THE PRODUCTION-UNCAPPED LIMITATION -- CONFIRMED STATED CLEARLY IN ALL FOUR LOCATIONS ===

  - Design section 0 (lines ~82-94): explicit, bulleted, same prominence as the native-leak limitation, states "DOES NOT cap production WASM dispatch" and "no production call site acquires a lease, because none exists yet."
  - Design section 7's REQUIRED moduledoc content (lines ~812-823): a full paragraph, positioned BEFORE the native-leak limitation paragraph (i.e. equal-or-greater prominence, not buried after it), states "PRODUCTION WASM DISPATCH DOES NOT CALL THIS MODULE YET" in caps, names the only current callers as the :wasm_hang tests, and states plainly "A real WASM guest invocation reached by production dispatch is therefore admitted with NO cap of any kind today." A future maintainer reading ONLY the shipped module's own moduledoc (not this design doc) would receive this limitation with at least as much prominence as any other claim in the moduledoc -- this satisfies the check's own stated concern ("the moduledoc is what a future maintainer reads").
  - Design section 6.6: requires an explicit per-test-file comment ("this lease is test-side only; production dispatch does not acquire one yet") on the new wiring itself, so a reader of the TEST file also sees the limitation, not only a reader of the module or the design doc.
  - Design section 9, OQ-C and OQ-D: both restate the limitation in the open-questions section, and OQ-D's closing line is explicit: "production remains uncapped despite the CI flake being addressed."
  No location found, in any of these four, that could be read by a future maintainer as claiming production is protected. PASS, no finding.

=== 5. ITEMS NOT RE-LITIGATED, SPOT-CHECKED FOR REWORK-2 DISTURBANCE ===

Lease placement outside the kill boundary (S2/S8.1): unchanged in substance from the reviewed-and-passed rework-1 text; S6.2's test-side application is a faithful extension of the same reasoning (verified above under item 3), not a new claim requiring re-derivation from scratch. Monitor backstop (S5.3/S5.4): unchanged; the SandboxPool line-number citations were already corrected in this rework (sandbox_pool.ex:566, matching my own prior finding) -- confirmed fixed, no longer citing :567. New-primitive justification (S3): unchanged prose, no new claim introduced. S0/S7 honesty content: the prior PASS holds for the native-leak-vs-cap-scope distinction; the NEW production-uncapped content layered on top in this rework is covered fully under item 4 above. No disturbance found requiring full re-derivation of any of these four areas.

=== THE BLOCKER: SECTION 6.3.1's OWN ARITHMETIC, APPLIED TO ISS-0418's OWN CITED CI RUNNER, PREDICTS THE FLAKE PERSISTS ===

Section 6.3.1 names a real residual risk (cumulative sequential leaks exceeding a small runner's total pool size) and then argues it away as merely theoretical: "no recurrence note in ISS-0418's own record describes a failure shape consistent with ran out of pool slots despite perfectly serial admission." This reasoning does not hold up under re-derivation using the design's OWN cited numbers.

ISS-0418's own recurrence evidence (docs/issues/ISS-0418.yaml:183, quoted directly): "All three ran on the same commit, on GitHub's ubuntu-latest (N=4 vCPU)" -- the ACTUAL CI runner this whole issue is about. This design's own section 5.5 states explicitly, in its OWN justification for the production default formula, that on "a small CI runner (~4 vCPU, ISS-0418's own recurrence evidence, where the two counts typically track 1:1 on a dedicated runner)" -- i.e. the design ITSELF asserts available_parallelism() is ~4 on this exact runner. Section 6.1 confirms this same design wires 8 sequential, permanently-unrecoverable native-thread leaks into one `mix test --only wasm_hang` subprocess run.

8 leaks against a ~4-slot pool, using the design's own numbers: by dispatch #5, the pool is already fully consumed by dispatches #1-4's permanent leaks (§0/§4's own confirmed-unbounded, confirmed-unrecoverable-within-90s finding, unchanged and undisputed by this rework) -- REGARDLESS of how perfectly serialized admission is, because §6.3 itself states the serialization property only bounds SIMULTANEOUS admission, never grows the pool back between dispatches. Dispatches #5 through #8 would then be attempting to dispatch into a pool with zero free native slots, which -- per this design's OWN §0 finding, unchanged since the original diagnosis -- is exactly the failure mode ISSUE-FIXER live-reproduced ("a subsequently-dispatched trivial non-hanging guest call did not return within 90,000ms"). A NEW guest invocation attempted against an exhausted pool does not fail cleanly with {:error, :capacity} (that is InvocationLease's OWN synthetic error, gating ADMISSION, not the native call) -- it HANGS, indistinguishably from the very failure ISS-0418 exists to fix, because the native Wasmtime call itself has nowhere to run. This means dispatches #5-8 in the ACTUAL isolated wasm_hang subprocess, on the ACTUAL GitHub ubuntu-latest runner this issue's own evidence is drawn from, are predicted BY THIS DESIGN'S OWN ARITHMETIC to still hang and still fail -- the identical ExUnit.TimeoutError-after-180000ms class recorded in EVERY recurrence note in ISS-0418.yaml, just relocated from a concurrent-contention trigger to a sequential-exhaustion trigger.

Section 6.3.1's own defense ("no recurrence note describes a failure shape consistent with sequential exhaustion") is not evidence this residual risk is small -- it is exactly what you would expect to see BEFORE this fix ships, because every recurrence to date failed via CONCURRENT contention (multiple wasm_hang tests racing) before ever reaching a state where sequential-only exhaustion could be observed in isolation. Removing the concurrent-contention failure mode (this rework's genuine, confirmed achievement, item 1 above) does not remove the underlying leak count -- it exposes the SAME exhausted-pool state through a different, previously-masked path, which the design's own §6.3.1 numbers already predict. ORCH's own stated reason for choosing option three ("the CI gate measures 44% with every classifiable failure being this flake... a primitive proven not to touch that call graph would leave the run's stated justification unmet") is exactly the outcome this finding says is still likely: after this design ships, the isolated wasm_hang subprocess run on real GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runners is predicted, by the design's own cited pool-size figure, to still fail via timeout on a meaningful fraction of runs -- not because concurrency was not fixed (it was, genuinely), but because 8 permanent leaks was never going to fit inside a ~4-slot pool no matter how they are sequenced.

This is not a hypothetical edge case the grading instruction says to record as MINOR ("reserve BLOCKER/MAJOR for something that would actually ship broken"). It directly attacks the premise ORCH's own message states this scope expansion exists to satisfy, using only numbers already inside this document and inside ISS-0418.yaml. If this reasoning is correct, merging this design as scoped will very likely leave the CI gate still red on real CI after implementation, exactly the "looks fixed, isn't" outcome section 6.0 itself invokes as the reason to take this option seriously. BLOCKER.

What would resolve this, stated concretely rather than left for CODE-DESIGNER to re-derive: either (a) reduce the suite's OWN total hang-dispatch footprint from 8 to at or below the smallest CI runner's actual pool size (the design's own §6.3.1 names this exact lever, "the same reduce genuine-hang footprint lever ISS-0352's original resolution already used once, from ~9 to ~7" -- but does not apply it, despite having the number needed to know it is required NOW, not merely as future contingency), or (b) verify empirically, before claiming this fixes the flake, what `available_parallelism()` actually is inside a fresh GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest wasm_hang subprocess (the design assumes ~4 by analogy to vCPU count but never states this was actually measured on that runner, only inferred), or (c) if the true pool size on that runner turns out to be materially larger than 4 for some undocumented reason (extra hyperthreading exposed to available_parallelism, e.g.), state that measurement explicitly as the basis for confidence rather than resting on ISS-0418.yaml's silence about a failure mode that could not have appeared until concurrent contention was already removed.

issues.finding: 8 sequential, permanent native-thread leaks are wired into the isolated wasm_hang subprocess in this rework, but ISS-0418's own recurrence evidence (docs/issues/ISS-0418.yaml:183) and this design's own §5.5 both state the real target CI runner (GitHub ubuntu-latest) has ~4 vCPU, implying an available_parallelism()-sized pool of ~4 in that fresh subprocess -- well below 8. By this design's own confirmed-unbounded, confirmed-unrecoverable leak model (§0/§4, unchanged), dispatches #5-8 in that subprocess run would be attempting to dispatch into an already-exhausted pool regardless of how well concurrent admission is serialized, and would hang exactly like every prior recurrence -- just via a sequential-exhaustion trigger the concurrent-contention fix newly exposes rather than masks. §6.3.1 dismisses this as theoretical on the ground that no PAST recurrence note shows this failure shape, but every past recurrence failed via concurrent contention first, which is exactly why a sequential-only failure could not yet have been observed -- that silence is not evidence of safety. This directly undermines ORCH's own stated reason for choosing this option (closing the 44%-failure CI gate) -- the design's own numbers predict the gate stays red on real CI after this ships. Required fix: reduce the suite's total hang-dispatch footprint to at or below the smallest real CI runner's actual measured pool size before claiming this design fixes the flake (§6.3.1 itself names this lever but does not apply it), or empirically measure available_parallelism() inside an actual GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest wasm_hang subprocess and state that measured number as the basis for confidence rather than an inferred vCPU-count analogy.

The original §8 code-shape sketch (wiring try_acquire/release inside handle_node/1) is still present verbatim in the document, marked superseded by §8.1 rather than removed. This was already true at the prior gate and the design explicitly instructs treating it as superseded, not conflicting -- noted here only so a future reader who skims §8 in isolation (skipping §8.1's correction) is not misled; consider deleting the stale sketch entirely in a future pass rather than leaving superseded content in the shipped design doc, but this does not block this gate since the document itself already flags the supersession clearly and this was accepted at the prior gate.

The corrected default-cap formula (max(div(schedulers_online(),2),1)) is now verified non-self-contradictory: re-derived against both cited hosts (16-vs-8 divergent host: div(16,2)=8, landing exactly AT the cited pool size of 8, boundary case as the design itself now states; this rework's own 16-vs-16 convergent host: div(16,2)=8, comfortably below 16) and against a ~4 vCPU CI runner (div(4,2)=2, below ~4). The design's own honest caveat (boundary case, not strictly protective, operator must override on divergent hosts) is accurate and not overclaimed. No finding beyond noting this MAJOR from the prior gate is genuinely resolved, recorded here for the traceability record rather than silently dropped.

Row 5 (plugin_handler_test.exs:353, REQ-170 AC1) was not quoted verbatim from the test body in this validation's direct read (only its sibling AC3/AC4 tests were read in full to confirm shapes); its call shape (single PluginInterface.invoke/2 call) was inferred from the design's own consistent table pattern and the file's own describe-block structure rather than independently re-quoted line-by-line. This is a lower-confidence spot versus the other six rows, which were read and confirmed directly against real source. Recorded as MINOR rather than left silent, per this project's own audit-trail discipline -- does not block this gate since nothing about this row's design treatment (Shape A, same as rows 2/4/7) is unusual or novel enough to carry material risk if the exact line contents differ slightly from the table.

next_action: Route back to CODE-DESIGNER (rework 3 of 3) to resolve the BLOCKER: either reduce the wasm_hang suite's total hang-dispatch footprint to at or below the smallest real CI runner's pool size, or obtain and cite an actual measurement of available_parallelism() inside a real GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest wasm_hang subprocess rather than relying on an inferred vCPU-count analogy. This is the final rework iteration (max_rework: 3) -- if this cannot be resolved within scope, escalate to ORCH per docs/agents/ORCHESTRATOR.md §5 rather than attempting a fourth rework.
